items.headline: ‘Is This Hilton?’ An Ad Blitz Answers: Yes, We Have Lifestyle Hotels
items.body: Hilton spent years buying and licensing non-traditional hotel brands. Its new ad campaign is the bill coming due: It has to teach travelers about the new places to stay.

items.headline: Prices Prop Up Travel as Demand Cools
items.body: Travel interest is slipping, but revenue is holding because prices are doing the work. That cushion only lasts as long as travelers keep paying more, which makes falling search activity worth watching closely heading into 2027.

items.headline: OpenAI Acquires Odessia, the AI Travel Agent From Sonder’s Co-Founder
items.body: OpenAI didn't acquire Odessia for its revenue. It bought a team that built a working AI travel agent in months, plus a founder who ran a lodging company, which included hotels and short-term rentals, for a decade. It's a sign ChatGPT wants to do more in travel than send users to Booking.com and Expedia.

items.headline: Japan Is Closing in on the U.S. as High Costs and Politics Deter Travelers, Brand USA Says
items.body: Research shows the U.S. losing ground to Japan as costs and politics turn travelers away. Brand USA is betting the lost demand is deferred, not gone, but its budget to win it back is shrinking.

items.headline: Hotel Chains’ Middle East Recovery Stalls as Peak Season Arrives
items.body: The Middle East is a small slice of most hotel chains’ revenue but a bigger part of their pipelines. So far, they’re holding to their development plans, even as a second weak peak season looms.

items.headline: Expedia’s $676 Million in Acquisitions Points to More B2B Buying
items.body: Expedia’s 2026 deals are a fraction of the nearly $6 billion it spent in 2015. But three acquisitions in nine months, plus CEO Ariane Gorin’s pledge to keep investing, signal that Expedia is a buyer again. And B2B is where the money is going.

items.headline: Dear Robot: How Travel Is (and Isn’t) Talking to AI
items.body: Travel brands invest deeply in AI visibility, but according to Skift's audit of 50 major travel websites' crawler policies, few tell bots where to go — and the directives don't always match who actually gets in. That looks like a shaky starting point, as the rules of AI engagement change.
